current_criteria.name: visual_grounding
current_criteria.description: How well the answer directly references or describes visible elements in the image. High grounding means the answer cites specific objects, positions, colors, or actions observable in the image. Low grounding includes vague or unsupported claims. Applicable to all visual QA questions.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer matches the actual content of the image without misrepresenting or distorting visual details. A correct answer accurately reflects what is seen; a factually inconsistent answer introduces errors or mislabeling. Critical for all visual QA tasks.

current_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinations
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer avoids fabricating or inventing visual details not present in the image. Hallucinations include adding objects, actions, or spatial relationships not shown — even if plausible. Annotators penalize hallucinations even if they seem reasonable.

current_criteria.name: question_relevance
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer directly addresses the question’s intent without drifting into unrelated or tangential information. A relevant answer focuses on what the question asks — e.g., describing composition vs. discussing unrelated background elements.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: How precisely and explicitly the answer describes visual elements — e.g., exact positions, sizes, textures, or interactions. Specific answers are more informative and less ambiguous than general or vague ones. Important for detailed visual descriptions.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer covers all relevant visual aspects addressed by the question without omitting key details. A complete answer doesn’t leave out major elements, even if they’re not central to the question’s intent.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer appropriately expresses uncertainty when visual evidence is ambiguous — e.g., using phrases like 'possibly,' 'might,' or 'likely' — rather than making definitive claims unsupported by the image. Annotators reward humility in ambiguous cases.

current_criteria.name: clear_language
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer is grammatically correct, concise, and easy to understand without ambiguity. Clear language improves interpretability and reduces miscommunication — especially important when comparing two answers.

current_criteria.name: consistency_in_description
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer maintains consistent terminology, spatial relationships, and object properties across all claims — e.g., if it says 'the cat is on the left,' it should not later say 'the cat is on the right.' Inconsistency reduces credibility.

current_criteria.name: plausibility_and_reasoning
current_criteria.description: Whether the answer is grounded in realistic or biologically/physically plausible visual logic — e.g., whether a zebra could see a lion from its left via peripheral vision, or whether an object’s position makes sense given gravity or perspective. Annotators favor answers that are both accurate and logically consistent with real-world knowledge.

manager_prompt:
List and describe 10 criteria for how human annotators compare the quality of two answers to the same visual question.

The task is RLHF-V style preference comparison for visual question answering and image-text responses. The worker model will receive:
- the image,
- the source question,
- candidate answer A,
- candidate answer B.

Focus on human preference factors such as visual grounding, question relevance, factual consistency with the image, avoidance of hallucinated visual details, completeness, specificity, calibrated uncertainty, and clear language.
